lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Word classes and noun categories
objectives: Distinguish common/proper and concrete/abstract nouns.
Identify pronouns, lexical verbs, auxiliaries and adjectives in context.
lessons.body:
A word's class depends on its job in a sentence. In “They paint the gate”, paint is a verb; in “The paint is wet”, paint is a noun. Nouns name people, places, things or ideas. A common noun names a category (city); a proper noun identifies a particular name (Ibadan). Concrete and abstract describe a different distinction: a stone is a material object; patience is a quality. Common is not the opposite of concrete.
Count nouns can be counted: one notebook, three notebooks. In ordinary usage, information and equipment are non-count: say “two pieces of information” and “some equipment”, not “informations”. Some nouns have count and non-count uses: chicken can name an animal or food. Learn irregular plurals from a dictionary: child/children, mouse/mice, parenthesis/parentheses, deer/deer. A compound usually pluralises its head: mother-in-law/mothers-in-law; head of state/heads of state.
Pronouns can replace a noun phrase: “Bola owns the bag. She carries it.” Use she as subject and her as object. Possessive determiners precede nouns (her bag); possessive pronouns stand alone (hers). An adjective describes a noun: a quiet room; the room is quiet. A lexical verb expresses the main event or state: “I know the answer.” Be, have and do can be lexical verbs or auxiliaries. In “She has finished”, has is auxiliary; in “She has a bicycle”, has is lexical. Modal auxiliaries such as can normally require a main verb in a complete verb phrase: can swim. Finite verbs carry tense or agreement; infinitives and participles are non-finite: to swim, swimming, written. Non-finite does not simply mean an -ing ending.
To analyse a sentence, find the main verb, ask who or what participates, then identify describing words and pronouns. Do not classify a word solely by its ending: childlike is an adjective despite ending in -like.

practice.question: Classify city, Ibadan, patience and stone using the distinctions taught.
practice.answer: city: common; Ibadan: proper; patience: abstract; stone: concrete.

practice.question: Explain the two uses of has in “She has a pen” and “She has written”.
practice.answer: The first is a lexical possession verb; the second is an auxiliary with the participle written.

practice.question: Correct “two informations” and “three mother-in-laws”.
practice.answer: two pieces of information; three mothers-in-law.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Phrases, clauses and sentence functions
objectives: Distinguish a phrase from a finite clause.
Identify subjects, objects and complements.
lessons.body:
A phrase is a unit built around a head: “the new library” is a noun phrase headed by library. In “The new library opens today”, the whole phrase is the subject. In “We visited the new library”, it is the direct object. “We gave the librarian a book” contains indirect object the librarian and direct object a book. In “The librarian is our neighbour”, our neighbour is a subject complement. In “They elected Ayo captain”, captain is an object complement; it describes Ayo, not the subject they.
A verb phrase can contain a main verb alone or auxiliaries: works; has worked; may have been working. A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition and its complement: in the room, after the lesson. Its function depends on context: “the book on the desk” modifies book, while “She studied in the room” tells where she studied.
Finite clauses contain a finite verb and usually a subject. “The bell rang” is a main clause. “when the bell rang” is subordinate. English also has non-finite clauses, so it is too strong to say every clause must have a finite verb. At this level, start by recognising finite examples. “What she wrote pleased us”: What she wrote is a noun clause functioning as subject. “We know that she arrived”: that she arrived is an object clause. “The girl who won smiled”: who won modifies girl and is a relative clause, not merely an adjective phrase. “We left because it was late”: because it was late gives a reason.
A simple sentence has one main clause; a compound has two or more coordinated main clauses; a complex sentence has a main and subordinate clause; a compound-complex combines both. Count clauses, not just the number of visible verbs: “Ada sings and dances” can have one subject and a coordinated verb phrase. Use punctuation with the grammatical structure: “It rained, but we stayed” differs from the comma splice “It rained, we stayed”.

practice.question: Identify the objects in “Bisi gave her brother a notebook”.
practice.answer: her brother is indirect object; a notebook is direct object.

practice.question: What does “who won” do in “The girl who won smiled”?
practice.answer: It is a relative clause modifying girl.

practice.question: Classify “We left because it was late” and explain.
practice.answer: Complex: one main clause plus a subordinate reason clause.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: English sound symbols and listening contrasts
objectives: Read a consistent phonemic notation.
Distinguish selected consonant and vowel contrasts without confusing letters with sounds.
lessons.body:
This lesson uses the conventional British teaching chart as a reference model, not a claim that all English accents sound identical. A phoneme symbol represents a sound; a spelling may represent different sounds in different words. Slashes mark a phonemic transcription. The length mark is ː, not an ordinary spelling colon.
The chart's pure vowels are /iː ɪ e æ ɑː ɒ ɔː ʊ uː ʌ ɜː ə/. Familiar examples include fleece, kit, dress, trap, palm, lot, thought, foot, goose, strut, nurse and the final sound of comma. A diphthong moves between vowel qualities: /eɪ/ day, /aɪ/ my, /ɔɪ/ boy, /aʊ/ now, /əʊ/ go, /ɪə/ near, /eə/ square and the traditional chart's /ʊə/ cure. Some modern accents merge or realise the last three differently; consult the same reference model throughout an exercise.
Voicing contrasts include /p b/, /t d/, /k g/, /f v/, /θ ð/, /s z/, /ʃ ʒ/ and /tʃ dʒ/. The remaining consonants are /m n ŋ h l r w j/. /t/ is the voiceless alveolar stop in ten; /k/ is the velar stop in cat. /j/ as in yes is voiced. /ŋ/ occurs at the end of sing; it is not the letter j. /ʒ/ occurs in measure and /dʒ/ in judge. Do not substitute a Cyrillic look-alike for these IPA characters.
Compare sip/zip and fine/vine; only the initial phoneme changes in each pair. Compare ship/sheep for /ɪ/ and /iː/: quality as well as duration matters. Two words rhyme when their final stressed vowel and the following sounds agree, as in light/night. Ride/site do not rhyme because /d/ and /t/ differ.
Listen to an authorised model, repeat, record yourself if permitted, and compare. Written answers establish symbol recognition, not certified pronunciation. The teacher's oral observation remains separate.

practice.question: Correct these descriptions: /k/ in ten; /j/ is voiceless; ride and site rhyme.
practice.answer: ten begins /t/; /j/ is voiced; ride and site have different final consonants.

practice.question: Give the contrasts in sip/zip and ship/sheep.
practice.answer: /s/ versus /z/; /ɪ/ versus /iː/.

practice.question: Describe a responsible way to check pronunciation.
practice.answer: Listen to a consistent authorised model and obtain oral feedback; a written quiz alone cannot certify speech.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Writing a respectful informal letter
objectives: Organise an informal letter.
Give advice without pressuring another person.
lessons.body:
An informal letter is written to someone with whom the writer has a personal relationship. Include an address and date where the task requires them, a suitable greeting, an opening that establishes the purpose, a developed body and an appropriate close such as “With best wishes” followed by your name. A precise examination format must come from the actual task rather than an invented universal rule.
Advice should respect the recipient's agency. If a fictional relative faces a difficult relationship decision, acknowledge the difficulty, avoid blame, and suggest trusted support. Do not tell someone to remain in an unsafe situation. The language-learning objective is coherent, considerate communication; it does not require the writer to endorse a harmful decision.
Model opening: “Dear Sade, Thank you for telling me how you feel. I am sorry this has been difficult. I hope you can talk with someone you trust and consider what is safe and right for you.” A second paragraph can offer practical help without making the decision for the recipient. Close warmly and check that every paragraph contributes to the purpose.

practice.question: List four structural parts of an informal letter.
practice.answer: Greeting, opening/purpose, developed body and personal close; address/date are also acceptable where required.

practice.question: Rewrite “You must stay whatever happens” as considerate advice.
practice.answer: Example: Please put your safety first and seek support from someone you trust while deciding what to do.

practice.question: Write a short letter encouraging a friend preparing for an examination.
practice.answer: Accept a relevant friendly opening, two practical suggestions and an appropriate close, expressed coherently.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Affixes and reliable word formation
objectives: Distinguish a base, prefix and suffix.
Form words without treating accidental letter sequences as affixes.
lessons.body:
A base is the form to which an affix is added. A prefix precedes it: un + kind gives unkind. A suffix follows it: kind + ness gives kindness. Some affixes change meaning, some change word class, and some mark grammar. Unkind is still an adjective; kindness is a noun. Books adds a plural ending; walked adds a past-tense ending. Do not confuse derivational endings such as -en in widen with a past-tense ending.
Useful prefixes include re- (again: rewrite), pre- (before: preview), post- (after: postgraduate), anti- (against: antisocial), inter- (between: interschool), and bi- (two: bilingual). The negative prefix varies: legal/illegal, possible/impossible, regular/irregular, correct/incorrect. These patterns do not license inventing a form for every word. Check a dictionary when unsure. Antenatal begins with ante-, meaning before; anti- is different. An apparent shared spelling is not sufficient evidence of the same root: comedy is not come plus a suffix.
Suffix examples are teach/teacher, enjoy/enjoyment, happy/happiness, harm/harmless and beauty/beautiful. Spelling can change: happy loses y before -ness and gains i. A final silent e commonly drops before -ing: write/writing; it is often retained before -ment: move/movement. Learn exceptions and accepted spelling varieties. Noticeable retains e to keep the soft c sound. One-syllable consonant-vowel-consonant bases often double a final consonant before a vowel suffix: stop/stopped. Longer words depend partly on stress: admit/admitted but visit/visited. Do not apply this mechanically to w, x or y.
Analyse the intended meaning first, choose a real word, then check spelling and word class in a sentence. “She spoke clearly” needs an adverb; “Her explanation was clear” needs an adjective.

practice.question: Form nouns from happy and enjoy, and identify the suffix.
practice.answer: happiness (-ness); enjoyment (-ment).

practice.question: Correct “anti-natal”, “writeing” and “comedy is come plus -dy”.
practice.answer: antenatal; writing; comedy is not formed from the verb come in this way.

practice.question: Use harmless and rewrite in meaningful sentences.
practice.answer: Example: The mark is harmless. Please rewrite the unclear sentence.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Reading details, inference, scanning and summary with an original passage
objectives: Locate facts and make supported inferences.
Distinguish skimming from scanning.
Summarise without inventing facts.
lessons.body:
This is a newly authored equivalent activity, not a reproduction of a missing textbook passage or a past examination.
Passage — The library timetable
The school library used to open only during the lunch break. Mariam noticed that students who helped serve lunch often arrived just as the door closed. She counted visits for five days and asked classmates when they could attend. Their answers suggested that a short period after lessons would help. The librarian agreed to try two afternoon sessions, on Tuesday and Thursday, for three weeks. Students had to return borrowed books by the following Monday. During the trial, visits increased, but the room became noisy near the entrance. Two volunteers moved the returns box away from the reading tables and placed a clear sign beside it. At the end of the trial, the librarian kept the afternoon sessions and asked the volunteers to continue recording visits. Mariam did not claim that every problem had been solved; she recommended checking whether students who travelled far could also benefit.
Skim by looking quickly for the overall topic and purpose. Here, the passage describes a trial that made a library more accessible. Scan for a particular fact: the sessions were Tuesday and Thursday, not every afternoon. Then read closely to understand relationships. The phrase “just as the door closed” explains why lunchtime access failed for some students. It is reasonable to infer that the old timetable was inconvenient for lunch helpers; it is not reasonable to infer that they disliked reading.
For context vocabulary, substitute a candidate meaning and reread: trial means a temporary test here, not a court proceeding. Main ideas explain the problem, response and result. A summary leaves out illustrative details while preserving these relationships. In two sentences: “The school tested afternoon library sessions to help pupils who could not attend at lunchtime. Visits increased, and the librarian retained the sessions while arranging further monitoring.” This is a model answer for this activity, not an examination board's universal marking rule. Follow the word or sentence limit given in each question.

practice.question: Which days had afternoon sessions, and when were books due?
practice.answer: Tuesday and Thursday; the following Monday.

practice.question: Why is “the students disliked reading” an unsupported inference?
practice.answer: The passage reports inconvenient opening times, not dislike of reading.

practice.question: Explain trial in context and summarise the outcome in one sentence.
practice.answer: Trial means a temporary test. Example summary: Afternoon access increased visits and was retained with continued monitoring.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Synonyms, antonyms and contextual choice
objectives: Choose a synonym that preserves meaning in context.
Distinguish gradable and complementary opposites.
lessons.body:
Near-synonyms overlap in meaning but are not interchangeable everywhere. A portrait represents a person; a sketch may be a quick outline; a print is a reproduced image. Paint is the colouring material or an action, not the name for a printed copy. In “a bright pupil”, bright can mean intelligent; in “a bright lamp”, it concerns light. Substitute a candidate, check grammar and then check the intended sense. Reject and emit are not general synonyms.
Antonyms express an opposition in a particular sense. Gradable opposites admit intermediate values: hot/cold with warm between them. Comparative forms such as hotter express degree; they are not the definition of gradable antonymy. Complementary opposites divide a stated domain into mutually exclusive alternatives, such as present/absent on a simple attendance register. Real-world categories may need qualifications, so do not treat married/single as an exhaustive description of everyone's status. Converse terms express a relationship from different viewpoints: buy/sell, parent/child.
Affixes sometimes form opposites: possible/impossible, legal/illegal, kind/unkind. The choice is conventional; do not invent a prefix for every word. Use a dictionary for an unfamiliar sense and check a complete sentence.

practice.question: Explain why bright cannot always be replaced with intelligent.
practice.answer: Bright describes light in some contexts and intelligence in others; only the latter sense permits the substitution.

practice.question: Give a gradable pair and a converse pair.
practice.answer: hot/cold; buy/sell.

practice.question: Correct “a paint is a copied picture” and “reject means emit”.
practice.answer: A print can be a reproduced picture; reject means refuse or dismiss in relevant contexts, not generally emit.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Adverbs and tense in context
objectives: Use adverbs with suitable verb forms.
Distinguish simple, continuous and perfect forms.
lessons.body:
An adverb can modify a verb, adjective or another adverb: runs quickly; very careful; quite slowly. Many manner adverbs end in -ly, but fast and hard do not. Hardly usually means almost not, not “with great effort”. Well is the usual adverb corresponding to good. A sentence adverb can express the speaker's view: “Fortunately, the bus arrived.” A linking adverb connects ideas: “It rained; however, the match continued.” It is not punctuated like the coordinating conjunction but.
The simple present expresses habits or general situations: “She reads after school.” The present continuous uses am/is/are plus -ing for an ongoing or temporary activity: “She is reading now.” The simple past places an event in a finished past period: “She read yesterday.” The present perfect uses has/have plus a past participle and relates a past event or continuing situation to the present: “She has finished”; “She has lived here for two years.” It is not restricted to things that have just happened. The past perfect uses had plus a past participle for an earlier past event: “She had left before the rain began.” The present perfect continuous uses has/have been plus -ing: “She has been reading for an hour.”
Choose the form from the intended time relationship. In ordinary usage, “She has finished yesterday” conflicts with the finished past time; use “She finished yesterday.” A phrase such as for two years can fit different tenses depending on whether the period is continuing or finished. Do not decide from one cue word alone.

practice.question: Correct “She has finished yesterday” and “He worked hardly” when he made a great effort.
practice.answer: She finished yesterday. He worked hard.

practice.question: Explain “She had left before the rain began”.
practice.answer: Leaving happened earlier than the beginning of the rain; had left is past perfect.

practice.question: Write one habitual and one ongoing sentence using read.
practice.answer: She reads every evening. She is reading now.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Planning four essay types
objectives: Distinguish narrative, descriptive, expository and argumentative purposes.
Build a coherent paragraph and an evidence-based argument.
lessons.body:
An essay's purpose determines its organisation. A narrative recounts linked events, usually with a setting, participants, a difficulty, a turning point and an outcome. Choose a consistent viewpoint and use time links rather than a list of unrelated events. A descriptive essay creates a precise impression of a person, place or event. Select relevant sensory details and arrange them spatially or by importance; description need not invent facts about a real person.
An expository essay explains a subject or process. Define important terms, organise the explanation into stages or reasons, and illustrate it. For “How our class can reduce paper waste”, a plan could explain the problem, introduce shared drafts, explain reusing one-sided sheets, and discuss monitoring results. An argumentative essay advances a defensible position. State a claim, supply reasons and examples, consider a counterargument, and reach a conclusion. A claim is not proved merely by repeating it. Avoid making invented statistics look like evidence.
Model argumentative paragraph: “A quiet reading period should remain on the timetable because it gives students uninterrupted practice. For example, pupils can finish a short text and discuss its main idea afterwards. Some may prefer free conversation, but that can be scheduled separately. A short protected period balances both needs.” The example is hypothetical, not a research result.
Write a plan before drafting. Each paragraph should develop one point with explanation; link paragraphs so the reader can follow the sequence. Revise for relevance, clarity, grammar and spelling. A proverb-based story may illustrate or question a saying: it need not endorse discrimination. Describe a character's belief as that character's belief, not a universal truth about men or women.

practice.question: Choose a suitable type for explaining a process and for recounting an incident.
practice.answer: Expository for a process; narrative for an incident.

practice.question: Give a claim, counterargument and response about a school reading period.
practice.answer: Example: Keep a reading period; some prefer conversation; timetable both activities separately.

practice.question: Write an 80–120-word paragraph explaining one way to reduce paper waste.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: English sound symbols and listening contrasts
objectives: Read a consistent phonemic notation.
Distinguish selected consonant and vowel contrasts without confusing letters with sounds.
lessons.body:
This lesson uses the conventional British teaching chart as a reference model, not a claim that all English accents sound identical. A phoneme symbol represents a sound; a spelling may represent different sounds in different words. Slashes mark a phonemic transcription. The length mark is ː, not an ordinary spelling colon.
The chart's pure vowels are /iː ɪ e æ ɑː ɒ ɔː ʊ uː ʌ ɜː ə/. Familiar examples include fleece, kit, dress, trap, palm, lot, thought, foot, goose, strut, nurse and the final sound of comma. A diphthong moves between vowel qualities: /eɪ/ day, /aɪ/ my, /ɔɪ/ boy, /aʊ/ now, /əʊ/ go, /ɪə/ near, /eə/ square and the traditional chart's /ʊə/ cure. Some modern accents merge or realise the last three differently; consult the same reference model throughout an exercise.
Voicing contrasts include /p b/, /t d/, /k g/, /f v/, /θ ð/, /s z/, /ʃ ʒ/ and /tʃ dʒ/. The remaining consonants are /m n ŋ h l r w j/. /t/ is the voiceless alveolar stop in ten; /k/ is the velar stop in cat. /j/ as in yes is voiced. /ŋ/ occurs at the end of sing; it is not the letter j. /ʒ/ occurs in measure and /dʒ/ in judge. Do not substitute a Cyrillic look-alike for these IPA characters.
Compare sip/zip and fine/vine; only the initial phoneme changes in each pair. Compare ship/sheep for /ɪ/ and /iː/: quality as well as duration matters. Two words rhyme when their final stressed vowel and the following sounds agree, as in light/night. Ride/site do not rhyme because /d/ and /t/ differ.
Listen to an authorised model, repeat, record yourself if permitted, and compare. Written answers establish symbol recognition, not certified pronunciation. The teacher's oral observation remains separate.

practice.question: Correct these descriptions: /k/ in ten; /j/ is voiceless; ride and site rhyme.
practice.answer: ten begins /t/; /j/ is voiced; ride and site have different final consonants.

practice.question: Give the contrasts in sip/zip and ship/sheep.
practice.answer: /s/ versus /z/; /ɪ/ versus /iː/.

practice.question: Describe a responsible way to check pronunciation.
practice.answer: Listen to a consistent authorised model and obtain oral feedback; a written quiz alone cannot certify speech.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Affixes and reliable word formation
objectives: Distinguish a base, prefix and suffix.
Form words without treating accidental letter sequences as affixes.
lessons.body:
A base is the form to which an affix is added. A prefix precedes it: un + kind gives unkind. A suffix follows it: kind + ness gives kindness. Some affixes change meaning, some change word class, and some mark grammar. Unkind is still an adjective; kindness is a noun. Books adds a plural ending; walked adds a past-tense ending. Do not confuse derivational endings such as -en in widen with a past-tense ending.
Useful prefixes include re- (again: rewrite), pre- (before: preview), post- (after: postgraduate), anti- (against: antisocial), inter- (between: interschool), and bi- (two: bilingual). The negative prefix varies: legal/illegal, possible/impossible, regular/irregular, correct/incorrect. These patterns do not license inventing a form for every word. Check a dictionary when unsure. Antenatal begins with ante-, meaning before; anti- is different. An apparent shared spelling is not sufficient evidence of the same root: comedy is not come plus a suffix.
Suffix examples are teach/teacher, enjoy/enjoyment, happy/happiness, harm/harmless and beauty/beautiful. Spelling can change: happy loses y before -ness and gains i. A final silent e commonly drops before -ing: write/writing; it is often retained before -ment: move/movement. Learn exceptions and accepted spelling varieties. Noticeable retains e to keep the soft c sound. One-syllable consonant-vowel-consonant bases often double a final consonant before a vowel suffix: stop/stopped. Longer words depend partly on stress: admit/admitted but visit/visited. Do not apply this mechanically to w, x or y.
Analyse the intended meaning first, choose a real word, then check spelling and word class in a sentence. “She spoke clearly” needs an adverb; “Her explanation was clear” needs an adjective.

practice.question: Form nouns from happy and enjoy, and identify the suffix.
practice.answer: happiness (-ness); enjoyment (-ment).

practice.question: Correct “anti-natal”, “writeing” and “comedy is come plus -dy”.
practice.answer: antenatal; writing; comedy is not formed from the verb come in this way.

practice.question: Use harmless and rewrite in meaningful sentences.
practice.answer: Example: The mark is harmless. Please rewrite the unclear sentence.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Word stress, intonation and dictionary use
objectives: Locate stress with a consistent dictionary model.
Explain how intonation changes pragmatic meaning.
lessons.body:
Word stress is prominence within a word. It can be marked by ˈ before a stressed syllable in IPA. Some noun/verb pairs shift stress, such as a REcord and to reCORD, but this is not a rule for every two-syllable word. Consent does not automatically shift because its word class changes. Check a reliable pronunciation dictionary and listen to the same variety used in class.
Sentence prominence highlights information: “BOLA borrowed the book” contrasts the borrower; “Bola BORROWED the book” contrasts borrowing with another action. In a response question, choose the alternative that contrasts the highlighted element rather than changing an unrelated fact.
Intonation is movement of pitch across an utterance. Questions and requests do not all have one compulsory tune. “Could you open the window, please?” may use a polite rise or a fall-rise depending on context. A direct command such as “Get out” is not automatically a polite request. Teach recognition through a model recording and actual interaction, not a blank printed arrow. A dictionary entry can show spelling, word class, pronunciation, meanings and examples. The apostrophe-like stress mark and syllable divisions must be read carefully; spelling alone cannot supply stress.
For practice, choose a word, read its pronunciation entry, listen, mark the stressed syllable, then use it in a sentence. Written identification and oral production are different assessment outcomes.

practice.question: Why is “all two-syllable nouns stress the first syllable” unsafe as a rule?
practice.answer: It overgeneralises; stress is lexical and exceptions require dictionary/model checks.

practice.question: What contrast is suggested by “BOLA borrowed the book”?
practice.answer: Bola rather than another person borrowed it.

practice.question: Turn “Get out” into a considerate request in a suitable context.
practice.answer: Example: Could you wait outside for a moment, please? Tone and context still matter.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Phrases, clauses and sentence functions
objectives: Distinguish a phrase from a finite clause.
Identify subjects, objects and complements.
lessons.body:
A phrase is a unit built around a head: “the new library” is a noun phrase headed by library. In “The new library opens today”, the whole phrase is the subject. In “We visited the new library”, it is the direct object. “We gave the librarian a book” contains indirect object the librarian and direct object a book. In “The librarian is our neighbour”, our neighbour is a subject complement. In “They elected Ayo captain”, captain is an object complement; it describes Ayo, not the subject they.
A verb phrase can contain a main verb alone or auxiliaries: works; has worked; may have been working. A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition and its complement: in the room, after the lesson. Its function depends on context: “the book on the desk” modifies book, while “She studied in the room” tells where she studied.
Finite clauses contain a finite verb and usually a subject. “The bell rang” is a main clause. “when the bell rang” is subordinate. English also has non-finite clauses, so it is too strong to say every clause must have a finite verb. At this level, start by recognising finite examples. “What she wrote pleased us”: What she wrote is a noun clause functioning as subject. “We know that she arrived”: that she arrived is an object clause. “The girl who won smiled”: who won modifies girl and is a relative clause, not merely an adjective phrase. “We left because it was late”: because it was late gives a reason.
A simple sentence has one main clause; a compound has two or more coordinated main clauses; a complex sentence has a main and subordinate clause; a compound-complex combines both. Count clauses, not just the number of visible verbs: “Ada sings and dances” can have one subject and a coordinated verb phrase. Use punctuation with the grammatical structure: “It rained, but we stayed” differs from the comma splice “It rained, we stayed”.

practice.question: Identify the objects in “Bisi gave her brother a notebook”.
practice.answer: her brother is indirect object; a notebook is direct object.

practice.question: What does “who won” do in “The girl who won smiled”?
practice.answer: It is a relative clause modifying girl.

practice.question: Classify “We left because it was late” and explain.
practice.answer: Complex: one main clause plus a subordinate reason clause.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Synonyms, antonyms and contextual choice
objectives: Choose a synonym that preserves meaning in context.
Distinguish gradable and complementary opposites.
lessons.body:
Near-synonyms overlap in meaning but are not interchangeable everywhere. A portrait represents a person; a sketch may be a quick outline; a print is a reproduced image. Paint is the colouring material or an action, not the name for a printed copy. In “a bright pupil”, bright can mean intelligent; in “a bright lamp”, it concerns light. Substitute a candidate, check grammar and then check the intended sense. Reject and emit are not general synonyms.
Antonyms express an opposition in a particular sense. Gradable opposites admit intermediate values: hot/cold with warm between them. Comparative forms such as hotter express degree; they are not the definition of gradable antonymy. Complementary opposites divide a stated domain into mutually exclusive alternatives, such as present/absent on a simple attendance register. Real-world categories may need qualifications, so do not treat married/single as an exhaustive description of everyone's status. Converse terms express a relationship from different viewpoints: buy/sell, parent/child.
Affixes sometimes form opposites: possible/impossible, legal/illegal, kind/unkind. The choice is conventional; do not invent a prefix for every word. Use a dictionary for an unfamiliar sense and check a complete sentence.

practice.question: Explain why bright cannot always be replaced with intelligent.
practice.answer: Bright describes light in some contexts and intelligence in others; only the latter sense permits the substitution.

practice.question: Give a gradable pair and a converse pair.
practice.answer: hot/cold; buy/sell.

practice.question: Correct “a paint is a copied picture” and “reject means emit”.
practice.answer: A print can be a reproduced picture; reject means refuse or dismiss in relevant contexts, not generally emit.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Reading details, inference, scanning and summary with an original passage
objectives: Locate facts and make supported inferences.
Distinguish skimming from scanning.
Summarise without inventing facts.
lessons.body:
This is a newly authored equivalent activity, not a reproduction of a missing textbook passage or a past examination.
Passage — The library timetable
The school library used to open only during the lunch break. Mariam noticed that students who helped serve lunch often arrived just as the door closed. She counted visits for five days and asked classmates when they could attend. Their answers suggested that a short period after lessons would help. The librarian agreed to try two afternoon sessions, on Tuesday and Thursday, for three weeks. Students had to return borrowed books by the following Monday. During the trial, visits increased, but the room became noisy near the entrance. Two volunteers moved the returns box away from the reading tables and placed a clear sign beside it. At the end of the trial, the librarian kept the afternoon sessions and asked the volunteers to continue recording visits. Mariam did not claim that every problem had been solved; she recommended checking whether students who travelled far could also benefit.
Skim by looking quickly for the overall topic and purpose. Here, the passage describes a trial that made a library more accessible. Scan for a particular fact: the sessions were Tuesday and Thursday, not every afternoon. Then read closely to understand relationships. The phrase “just as the door closed” explains why lunchtime access failed for some students. It is reasonable to infer that the old timetable was inconvenient for lunch helpers; it is not reasonable to infer that they disliked reading.
For context vocabulary, substitute a candidate meaning and reread: trial means a temporary test here, not a court proceeding. Main ideas explain the problem, response and result. A summary leaves out illustrative details while preserving these relationships. In two sentences: “The school tested afternoon library sessions to help pupils who could not attend at lunchtime. Visits increased, and the librarian retained the sessions while arranging further monitoring.” This is a model answer for this activity, not an examination board's universal marking rule. Follow the word or sentence limit given in each question.

practice.question: Which days had afternoon sessions, and when were books due?
practice.answer: Tuesday and Thursday; the following Monday.

practice.question: Why is “the students disliked reading” an unsupported inference?
practice.answer: The passage reports inconvenient opening times, not dislike of reading.

practice.question: Explain trial in context and summarise the outcome in one sentence.
practice.answer: Trial means a temporary test. Example summary: Afternoon access increased visits and was retained with continued monitoring.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Noun forms: plurals, possessives, collectives and special cases
objectives: Form regular, irregular, compound and zero plurals and spell noun-forming endings correctly.
Capitalise proper nouns and form possessive nouns correctly.
Use count, non-count, collective and plural-only nouns with the right verb agreement.
lessons.body:
Features of a noun. A noun can usually be made plural, can follow a determiner such as a, the, this or those, can be described by an adjective, and can show possession. In “those tall girls”, girls is the noun, those is a determiner and tall is an adjective. Many nouns are built from other words by an ending: arrive/arrival, move/movement, kind/kindness, child/childhood, friend/friendship, art/artist, active/activity. Common noun-forming endings are -age, -ment, -ness, -hood, -ship, -ist, -ism, -ity, -cy, -tion, -ery, -er/-or, -ster, -tude and -ocracy (democracy). Treat endings as clues, not proof: -al and -like usually build adjectives (national, childlike), and the noun arrival is an exception. Check spelling when you add an ending: firm + ness = firmness, not firmess.
Capital letters. A proper noun names one particular person, place, institution or time and begins with a capital letter: Adaeze, Lagos, River Niger, Monday, March, Yoruba. A common noun does not unless it starts a sentence: a girl, the river, a day. Days, months, languages and nationalities are capitalised; seasons are not. A title is capitalised when it goes with a name (Dr Okoro, Chief Bello) but not on its own (the doctor).
Regular plurals. Most nouns add -s: book, books. Add -es after s, x, z, ch and sh: bus, buses; box, boxes; church, churches; dish, dishes. After a consonant, y changes to ies: city, cities; after a vowel it just adds s: day, days. Nouns ending in consonant + o often take -es (tomato, tomatoes; hero, heroes) but some take only -s (photo, piano). Most nouns ending in f or fe add -s (roof, roofs; chief, chiefs); a few change to -ves (leaf, leaves; knife, knives; life, lives). If unsure, check a dictionary.
Count and non-count nouns. Count nouns have a plural and take a number: one chair, four chairs. Non-count nouns name a mass or a whole and normally have no plural form: furniture, luggage, baggage, equipment, machinery, jewellery, stationery, advice, information, rice. Use a unit to count them: two items of furniture, a piece of advice, three bags of rice, a sheet of paper. These words take a singular verb: “The luggage is heavy.” Be careful with meaning change: damage (harm) is non-count, but damages means money a court orders someone to pay for harm. “The flood did a lot of damage”; “The court awarded damages.”
Collective nouns. A collective noun names a group as one thing: team, class, committee, family, band, troupe, herd, flock, crowd, a bevy of girls. When the group acts as one unit, use a singular verb: “The class is ready.” When you are thinking of the members acting separately, British usage often accepts a plural verb: “The class are choosing their seats.” Choose one pattern and keep it consistent in a sentence. Note that soldiers is an ordinary plural noun; army is the collective noun.
Possessive nouns. Show ownership with an apostrophe. Add ’s to a singular noun: Bola’s bag, the teacher’s desk. Add only the apostrophe to a regular plural ending in s: the students’ books, the girls’ hostel. Add ’s to an irregular plural that does not end in s: children’s toys, women’s league. For a singular name ending in s, both James’s book and James’ book are accepted; stay consistent. For joint ownership add ’s to the last name only: Ade and Bisi’s shop. For things, an of-phrase is usual: the leg of the table. Do not use an apostrophe to make a plural (write two books, not two book’s), and its (belonging to it) has no apostrophe; it’s means it is.
Irregular plurals. Some nouns change inside: man, men; woman, women; foot, feet; goose, geese; mouse, mice; louse, lice; tooth, teeth. A few take -en: ox, oxen; child, children. Latin and Greek nouns keep their old patterns: crisis, crises; axis, axes; oasis, oases; parenthesis, parentheses; index, indices (indexes for a book list); larva, larvae; curriculum, curricula (curriculums also occurs); medium, media; symposium, symposia; formula, formulae or formulas; forum, forums (fora is rare). The usual plural of person is people.
Plurals of compound nouns. In most compounds the main noun takes the plural: mothers-in-law, heads of state, passers-by, step-sons or stepsons, churchgoers. If the compound has no noun to carry the plural, put -s at the end: grown-ups, lay-bys, take-aways. When man or woman identifies a person's gender before an occupation noun, both words normally change in the plural: women doctors, men nurses. This is not a rule for every word beginning with man- or woman-; for example, manholes has the ordinary plural ending.
Zero plurals. Some nouns have the same form in singular and plural: one sheep, two sheep; one deer, many deer; one aircraft, five aircraft; series, species, trout, salmon, fish. The verb or number shows which is meant: “The sheep is lame”; “The sheep are grazing.” Fish normally stays fish; fishes is used for different kinds of fish.
Nouns used mostly in the plural. Some nouns have a plural form and no singular in ordinary use and take a plural verb: cattle, goods, belongings, ashes, congratulations, manners, surroundings, wages, remains, clothes. Tools and clothes made of two parts are plural too: scissors, trousers, glasses; count them with pair: a pair of scissors. Headquarters and works name a place and may take a singular or plural verb (“The headquarters is in Abuja”; “The works are closed”); pick one pattern and keep to it. Cattle is plural in meaning; it is not a zero-plural noun, and aircraft is a zero-plural noun, not a plural-only noun. Take care with meaning: arm is a body part, but arms are weapons; a work is something made or done, and works can mean a factory or a writer’s output; quarters can mean lodgings.

practice.question: Write the plural of each noun and name the rule: city, church, day, leaf, tomato.
practice.answer: cities (consonant + y becomes ies); churches (-ch takes -es); days (vowel + y takes -s); leaves (f changes to -ves); tomatoes (consonant + o takes -es here).

practice.question: Rewrite with correct capital letters and say which words are proper nouns: “on tuesday, dr okoro travelled from enugu to the river niger with her yoruba teacher.”
practice.answer: “On Tuesday, Dr Okoro travelled from Enugu to the River Niger with her Yoruba teacher.” Proper nouns: Tuesday, Dr Okoro, Enugu, River Niger (Yoruba names a language and is capitalised).

marking.criterion: Dr Okoro capitalised as a title with a name

practice.question: Correct the errors without changing the intended meaning: (a) “The furnitures are new.” (b) “The court awarded him a damage.” (c) “Both team are ready.”
practice.answer: (a) The furniture is new (non-count). (b) The court awarded him damages (money). (c) Both teams are ready. Keep both: replacing it with the team changes two teams to one.

marking.criterion: Both teams are ready: plural teams preserves the meaning of both.

practice.answer: (a) the students’ books; (b) the children’s toys; (c) Ade and Bisi’s shop.

marking.criterion: joint ownership with ’s on the last name

practice.question: Give the plural of: mother-in-law, grown-up, woman doctor, crisis, curriculum.
practice.answer: mothers-in-law; grown-ups; women doctors; crises; curricula (curriculums also occurs).

practice.question: Choose the correct form and explain: (a) “Five (aircraft / aircrafts) landed.” (b) “The cattle (is / are) in the field.” (c) “Two (pair of scissors / pairs of scissors) were on the desk.”
practice.answer: (a) aircraft: zero plural. (b) are: cattle is plural in meaning. (c) pairs of scissors: count with pair.

practice.question: Explain why “soldiers” is not a good example of a collective noun, and give the collective noun that names the group.
practice.answer: Soldiers is an ordinary plural noun naming several individuals; a collective noun names the group as a unit, for example army.

marking.criterion: collective noun such as army or troop

practice.question: Form a noun from each word and spell it correctly: firm, friend, move, active.
practice.answer: firmness; friendship; movement; activity.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Pronouns, adjectives and verbs: types, kinds, formation and look-alike pairs
objectives: Name the eight pronoun types and choose the right pronoun in context.
Identify attributive and predicative adjectives and name the kinds of adjectives.
Form adjectives with -ical, -ic, -eous, -ious, -uous, -ive, -able/-ible, -al and -ial.
Use work/works, damage/damages and stationery/stationary correctly.
List the primary and modal auxiliaries and use them correctly.
Distinguish transitive from intransitive verbs.
lessons.body:
Pronoun types. A pronoun stands in for a noun or noun phrase so that you need not repeat it. Eight types are usually taught, sorted by the job each does. Personal pronouns name the speaker, the person spoken to, or the person or thing spoken about: I, you, he, she, it, we and they as subjects; me, you, him, her, it, us and them as objects (“They invited us”). Possessive pronouns show ownership and stand alone: mine, yours, his, hers, ours and theirs (“The red bag is hers”). The words my, your, her, our and their come before a noun (“her bag”); they are possessive determiners, also called possessive adjectives, not pronouns. Its is normally a possessive determiner (“The dog wagged its tail”) and never takes an apostrophe; it’s means it is or it has.
Demonstrative pronouns point something out and stand alone: this, that, these and those (“Those are ripe”); before a noun the same words are demonstrative adjectives (“those mangoes”). Interrogative pronouns begin a question about a person or thing: who, whom, whose, which and what (“Whose is this?”). Reflexive pronouns end in -self or -selves and send the action back to the subject: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, oneself, ourselves, yourselves and themselves (“She taught herself”); the same forms can add emphasis (“I myself saw it”). Write themselves, not theirselves, and himself, not hisself. Reciprocal pronouns, each other and one another, show a two-way action (“The twins help each other”). Compare “They blamed themselves” (each blamed his or her own self) with “They blamed each other”.
Relative pronouns join a describing clause to a noun: who, whom, whose, which and that (“The teacher who marked it is here”). Use who or whom for people, which for things, that for either, and whose for possession. Who, whom, whose and which are also interrogative, so decide by the job: a word that opens a question is interrogative; a word that joins a clause to a noun is relative. Indefinite pronouns refer to people or things without naming them: someone, somebody, something, anyone, anybody, anything, everyone, everybody, everything, nobody, no one and nothing, with words such as all, some, any, each, none, both, few, many and several. Those ending in -one, -body or -thing take a singular verb (“Everyone is present”).
Adjective position. An adjective describes or limits a noun. When it comes before the noun it is attributive: a red shirt, a gentle lady. When it follows a link verb such as be, seem, become, feel, look, sound, taste or smell and describes the subject, it is predicative: “The shirt is red”; “The lady seems gentle”. Most adjectives work in both positions. A few do not: main, chief and utter normally come only before a noun (the main road, not “the road is main”), while afraid, asleep and alone normally come only after a verb (“The baby is asleep”, but “the sleeping baby”).
Kinds of adjectives. Each kind answers a different question about the noun. Colour: a green basket, a black goat. Size: a big box, a long road. Age: an old man, a young tree. Shape: a round table, a rectangular field. Origin: Nigerian rice, Ghanaian cloth, a Canadian city (these begin with a capital letter). Number: one goat, twenty pupils. Demonstrative: this, that, these and those before a noun (that chair). Possessive: my, your, his, her, its, our and their before a noun (her umbrella). Distributive: each, every, either and neither pick out the members of a group one at a time (each candidate, every pupil, either answer). Older school lists also place some and any here, so expect to meet them under this heading. Many modern grammars call the demonstrative, possessive, distributive and number words determiners because they limit a noun rather than describe it. Learn both labels: the kinds above are the traditional school names.
Forming adjectives. Many adjectives are made by adding an ending to a noun, verb or other base. Nine endings to know, with examples: -ical (grammatical, historical, classical); -ic (hero, heroic; economy, economic); -eous (courage, courageous; advantage, advantageous); -ious (ambition, ambitious; infect, infectious); -uous (continue, continuous; strenuous, conspicuous); -ive (create, creative; attract, attractive); -able or -ible (comfort, comfortable; read, readable; sense, sensible; visible, edible); -al (nation, national; music, musical; digit, digital); and -ial, also spelt -cial or -tial (commerce, commercial; finance, financial; president, presidential). The base often changes a little: drop a silent e (create, creative), change y to i (envy, envious), but keep the e after c or g before -able (notice, noticeable; manage, manageable). Treat an ending as a clue, not proof: some words with these endings are nouns (a sedative, a critic, music). Some -ic and -ical pairs also differ in meaning: economic (about the economy) and economical (not wasteful); historic (important in history) and historical (about the past).
Look-alike pairs. Work is usually a non-count noun meaning effort or a job (“She has a lot of work to do”), and it is also a verb (“He works hard”). Works has several jobs. It is the -s form of the verb (“She works at the bank”). It is a noun for a factory or industrial site (“the cement works”, “the steelworks”) or for building and repair operations (“road works”). It is also the plural of work in the sense of a piece of writing, music or art (“Soyinka’s collected works”). If works follows a singular subject and tells what that subject does, it is the verb; if it names a place, operations or creations, it is a noun. Damage is a non-count noun for harm (“The flood did serious damage to the bridge”) and also a verb (“Smoke damages the lungs”); it has no plural in the sense of harm, so “damages” is wrong there. Damages is a noun for the money a court orders someone to pay for harm done (“The court awarded her damages”). Stationery, with -er, is the non-count noun for writing materials such as paper, pens and envelopes (“some stationery”). Stationary, with -ar, is an adjective meaning not moving (“The bus was stationary”). Memory aid: the e in stationery is for envelopes; the a in stationary is for at rest.
Auxiliary verbs. An auxiliary verb helps a main verb to form a tense, question, negative or passive, or to add a shade of meaning. The primary auxiliaries are be, have and do. Be: am, is, are, was, were, be, being, been (“She is reading”; “The gate was locked”). Have: have, has, had, having (“They have left”). Do: do, does, did (“Did he call?”; “I do not know”). These three can also be lexical (main) verbs: “She is a nurse”, “He has a bicycle”, “I did my homework”. Modal auxiliaries add ideas such as ability, permission, possibility, obligation or prediction. The central modals are can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would and must. Ought to goes with them, and need and dare are semi-modals: they behave like modals in questions and negatives (“Need I go?”; “He daren’t speak”) but are ordinary verbs in other uses (“She needs help”; “He dared to ask”). A modal has no -s form, no infinitive and no -ing form, is followed by the bare infinitive (can swim, must go; only ought takes to) and forms questions without do (“Can she swim?”). A modal does not stand alone as the only verb of a full sentence: “She can swim”, not “She can” (a short answer such as “I can” is the exception).
Transitive and intransitive verbs. A transitive verb is used with a direct object, the noun or pronoun that receives the action. After the verb ask “what?” or “whom?”: “Ada kicked the ball” (kicked what? the ball). An intransitive verb has no direct object: “The baby slept.” Words that say where, when or how are not objects, so “They arrived early” and “She slept in the room” are intransitive. Many verbs are used both ways, so judge the sentence, not the word alone: “She rang the bell” (transitive) and “The bell rang” (intransitive); “Mother cooked rice” and “Mother cooked for the guests”. Link verbs such as be, seem, become and look take a complement that describes or identifies the subject, not a direct object: “Bola became a doctor.” A sentence with a transitive verb can usually be turned into the passive (“The ball was kicked by Ada”); an intransitive verb cannot.

practice.question: Name the type of each pronoun in brackets: (a) [Those] are ripe. (b) [Who] called? (c) The pen is [mine]. (d) The girl [who] won the race is my cousin. (e) The pupils helped [each other]. (f) She taught [herself]. (g) [Everybody] is here. (h) [They] left early.
practice.answer: (a) demonstrative; (b) interrogative; (c) possessive; (d) relative; (e) reciprocal; (f) reflexive; (g) indefinite; (h) personal.

practice.question: Choose the correct word: (a) The red bag on the chair is (her/hers). (b) Is this (your/yours) pen? (c) The dog wagged (its/it’s) tail. (d) The two friends greeted (themselves/each other).
practice.answer: (a) hers (a possessive pronoun standing alone); (b) your (a possessive determiner before a noun); (c) its (possessive determiner; it’s means it is or it has); (d) each other (reciprocal: each greeted the other; themselves would mean each greeted his or her own self).

practice.question: State whether each adjective in brackets is attributive or predicative: (a) The [tall] boy waved. (b) The soup smells [delicious]. (c) We crossed the [main] road. (d) The baby is [asleep]. (e) Say why “an asleep baby” is not normally used and give a natural alternative.
practice.answer: (a) attributive; (b) predicative (after the link verb smells); (c) attributive (main normally comes only before a noun); (d) predicative; (e) asleep normally occurs only after a verb, so say “the sleeping baby” (or “a baby who is asleep”).

marking.criterion: (e) states that asleep is normally used only after a verb
(e) gives an acceptable alternative such as the sleeping baby

practice.question: Name the kind of each adjective in brackets: (a) a [round] table (b) [twelve] pupils (c) [that] chair (d) [her] umbrella (e) [Ghanaian] cloth (f) [each] candidate.
practice.answer: (a) shape; (b) number; (c) demonstrative; (d) possessive; (e) origin; (f) distributive.

practice.question: Form an adjective from each word and name the ending you used: grammar, hero, courage, ambition, continue, create, comfort, nation, finance.
practice.answer: grammatical (-ical); heroic (-ic); courageous (-eous); ambitious (-ious); continuous (-uous); creative (-ive, silent e dropped); comfortable (-able); national (-al); financial (-ial).

practice.question: Choose the right word: (a) The court ordered the company to pay (damage/damages) to the injured driver. (b) The flood did serious (damage/damages) to the bridge. (c) Mr Ojo (work/works) at the cement (work/works). (d) I have a lot of (work/works) to finish tonight. (e) Buy some (stationary/stationery): pens, pencils and paper. (f) The bus was (stationary/stationery) at the junction. (g) Soyinka’s collected (work/works) are in the library.
practice.answer: (a) damages (money paid as compensation); (b) damage (non-count noun for harm); (c) works (verb); works (a factory site); (d) work (non-count: tasks or effort); (e) stationery (writing materials); (f) stationary (not moving); (g) works (the plural of work in the sense of creative works).

practice.question: Write the auxiliary verb in each sentence and say whether it is primary or modal. If there is no auxiliary, say what the verb is. (a) She has finished. (b) You must wait. (c) They are singing. (d) Did he call? (e) We might arrive late. (f) He is a pilot.
practice.answer: (a) has: primary (have); (b) must: modal; (c) are: primary (be); (d) Did: primary (do); (e) might: modal; (f) no auxiliary: is is the main (lexical, link) verb.

marking.criterion: (f) no auxiliary; is is the main verb

practice.question: Correct each sentence and give the rule: (a) “She cans swim.” (b) “You should to rest.” (c) “He must goes.” (d) “Does she can sing?” (e) “You ought rest more.”
practice.answer: (a) She can swim (a modal has no -s form). (b) You should rest (a modal takes the bare infinitive, without to). (c) He must go (bare infinitive after a modal). (d) Can she sing? (a modal forms questions without do). (e) You ought to rest more (ought takes to).

practice.question: Say whether the verb in each sentence is transitive or intransitive. If it is neither, say what it is. (a) Ada kicked the ball. (b) The baby slept. (c) They arrived early. (d) She rang the bell. (e) The bell rang. (f) The farmer sells yams. (g) Bola became a doctor. (h) The door opened.
practice.answer: (a) transitive (object: the ball); (b) intransitive; (c) intransitive (early tells when, so it is not an object); (d) transitive (object: the bell); (e) intransitive; (f) transitive (object: yams); (g) a link verb: a doctor is a complement describing or identifying Bola, not a direct object; (h) intransitive.

marking.criterion: (g) link verb with a complement, not transitive

practice.answer: Sample: “Mother cooked rice.” (transitive; direct object: rice). “Mother cooked for the guests.” (intransitive; no direct object). Accept any correct pair.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Word meanings in context: clues, senses and figurative use
objectives: Infer the meaning of an unfamiliar word from definition, example, contrast and cause-and-effect clues in the sentence and paragraph.
Choose the sense of a familiar word that fits its grammatical class and its surroundings.
Distinguish literal from figurative use and state a contextual meaning with the words that support it.
lessons.body:
A word can carry more than one meaning, and a dictionary entry lists the possibilities. A reader's task is to decide which possibility the writer is using. The sentence and the paragraph supply the evidence for that decision, so the same word can mean different things in different places. In “The fisherman tied his canoe to the bank”, bank is the ground beside a river; in “She queued at the bank to deposit her savings”, bank is the financial institution. The words canoe and deposit decide the sense.
A four-step routine. First, read the whole sentence, then the sentence before and after it, because one sentence is rarely enough. Second, decide the word's grammatical class in this sentence: a noun, a verb, an adjective or another class. Third, look for a clue of one of the kinds described below. Fourth, state the meaning in your own words and test it by putting that phrase back into the sentence: if the sentence still says the same thing, the meaning fits. Keep the replacement in the same grammatical class, since a noun phrase cannot stand in for a verb.
Definition or restatement clue. The sentence itself explains the word, often after a comma, a dash, a colon or a bracket, or after the phrases that is, in other words, or or. “The clinic was closed because of an epidemic — a disease that spreads quickly among many people.” The dash introduces the explanation, so epidemic means a disease spreading quickly among many people. “The chairman, in other words the person who leads the meeting, called for order.” The restatement gives the meaning of chairman.
Example clue. A list of examples shows the group or category that a word belongs to. “Citrus fruits such as oranges, lemons and grapefruit contain vitamin C.” The examples show that citrus names a group of fruits rather than one fruit, so the word means a group of juicy fruits with thick skins. “The implements — hoes, cutlasses and spades — were locked in the store.” The list shows that implements are tools used for work, not the crops grown with them. Examples narrow the meaning but may not define it fully, so state the category that they share.
Contrast clue. A word is explained by placing it against its opposite, often with unlike, but, although, whereas, instead of or on the other hand. “Unlike his frugal brother, Emeka spent his whole allowance on the first day.” The contrast with spending everything at once shows that frugal means careful about spending. “Although the road was wide, the bridge was narrow.” The contrast between wide and narrow fixes both meanings. Find the opposite item first, then describe the unknown word as the other end of that opposition.
Cause and effect clue. The sentence gives a cause, a result or a purpose, often with because, since, so, therefore, as a result or in order to. “The path became waterlogged after two days of rain, so the pupils took another route.” The cause (rain) and the result (another route) together point to waterlogged meaning soaked with water. “The heat was so intense that the paint blistered.” The effect on the paint shows that blistered means formed bubbles on its surface. Say which link you used: cause to result, or result back to cause.
Word parts and general knowledge. Prefixes, roots and suffixes, together with what the paragraph is about, can support a guess. “The doctor was optimistic about her recovery” contains optim-, a root associated with hope, and the sentence reports a good expectation. “The team was overconfident” joins over- (too much) to confident. These clues are hints, not proof: inflammable means easily set on fire, not “not flammable”, and a casual remark is not a causal explanation. Check a word-part guess against the rest of the sentence before trusting it.
Choosing among the senses of a familiar word. Many common words have several related senses, and the words around them choose the sense. Sharp describes a cutting edge in “a sharp knife”, a sudden strong pain in “a sharp pain in her side”, a sour or strong taste in “a sharp taste of lime”, a large sudden change in “a sharp rise in prices”, and a quick noticing mind in “a sharp pupil”. Read the noun that the adjective describes and the topic of the sentence; do not write down the first sense you remember. The same care applies to homonyms, words with unrelated meanings such as bank, bat and match.
Grammar as a clue. The word's class in the sentence narrows its meaning. Record is a verb in “The referee will record the result” and a noun in “the school record”; light is an adjective in “a light bag” and a verb in “to light the lamp”. Articles such as a and the, auxiliaries such as will and can, and the position of the word show which class is in use. Decide the class first, then choose a meaning that fits that class.
Literal and figurative meaning. A word used literally carries its basic sense: “The classroom was cold” reports a low temperature. A word used figuratively carries a comparison or an image: “The classroom was a zoo” does not report animals but says that the room was noisy and disordered. Similes mark the comparison with like or as (“her smile was like sunshine”); metaphors state it directly; idioms are fixed expressions whose meaning cannot be worked out word by word (“he kicked the bucket” means he died). When the literal sense is impossible in the situation, look for the figurative idea that the writer intends, and state that idea rather than the picture. Not every everyday expression is figurative, so check before deciding.
Connotation and tone. Two words can share a basic meaning and still differ in the feeling they carry. Childlike is usually approving, while childish is usually disapproving; famous is neutral or approving, while notorious is disapproving; thrifty is approving, while stingy is not. Context shows the writer's attitude through the surrounding words and the situation. Report the attitude that the passage actually shows, and do not add a judgement of your own.
Writing the answer. Give three things: the word as it is used, its part of speech in that sentence, and its meaning in this passage as a short synonym or phrase, followed by the clue that supports it. For example: “Blistered (verb) — formed bubbles on the surface; clue: ‘the heat was so intense that’ gives the cause.” Do not copy a whole dictionary entry, which lists senses that the passage does not use. Do not give a synonym that you have not tested in the sentence. Do not name a clue that is not in the text: quote the words you relied on.
Worked example. Read this passage and the three analyses. “During the harmattan the water in the village well was brackish, and even the goats sniffed it and turned away. Mama Ngozi, who was never wasteful, poured it into a wide clay bowl, left it in the sun for a day and then strained it through clean cloth. By evening the sharp taste had gone. ‘Patience is a strainer,’ she told the children, laughing.” Brackish (adjective) means slightly salty and unpleasant to drink; the clue is the effect, since the goats sniffed the water and refused it. Wasteful (adjective) means using more than is needed; the clue is the contrast between that description and her careful, repeated use of the same water. Strainer (noun) means a thing used to separate solid pieces from a liquid; the clue is the action in strained it through clean cloth, and the ending -er marks a person or thing that performs an action. The last sentence uses strainer figuratively: patience is compared to a filter that clears the water, so the word means something that removes what is unwanted, not a kitchen object.

practice.question: “The council built a reservoir — a large store of water for the dry season.” What does reservoir mean here, and which kind of clue gives it?
practice.answer: A large store of water kept for the dry season. Clue: definition or restatement, because the words after the dash explain the noun.

marking.criterion: meaning: a large store of water for the dry season
clue named as definition or restatement after the dash

practice.question: “She bought stationery such as exercise books, pens and file jackets.” What does stationery mean, and which words are the clue?
practice.answer: Materials used for writing and office work. Clue: the examples after such as (exercise books, pens, file jackets) show the group of things meant.

marking.criterion: clue identified as the example list after such as

practice.question: “Unlike the previous tenant, who repaired every fault at once, the new tenant was negligent.” What does negligent mean, and what is the clue?
practice.answer: Careless about duties, failing to take proper care. Clue: the contrast with the previous tenant, who repaired every fault at once, introduced by Unlike.

marking.criterion: meaning: careless or failing to take proper care
clue identified as the contrast with the previous tenant

practice.question: “The gutter was choked with refuse, so rainwater flooded the road.” What does choked mean, and what is the clue?
practice.answer: Blocked, so that water could not pass through. Clue: the result, since the flooding shows that the gutter could not carry the water away.

marking.criterion: meaning: blocked or filled so that water cannot pass
clue identified as the result in the same sentence

practice.question: Give the part of speech and the meaning of light in each sentence: (a) “She carried a light bag.” (b) “The caretaker will light the lamp at dusk.” (c) “He ate a light meal before the match.”
practice.answer: (a) adjective — not heavy; (b) verb — to make something burn or give light; (c) adjective — small and easy to digest.

marking.criterion: (b) meaning: to make something burn or give light
(c) meaning: small and easy to digest

practice.question: Label each sentence literal or figurative, then give the intended meaning of the quoted expression: (a) “The whole school was on fire with excitement.” (b) “The dry grass caught fire and the shed burned.” (c) “He has a heart of stone.” (d) “The stone broke the window.”
practice.answer: (a) figurative — everyone was very excited; nothing was actually burning. (b) literal — the grass and the shed really burned. (c) figurative — he is unkind or shows no sympathy. (d) literal — a real stone broke the window.

marking.criterion: (b) meaning: the grass and shed really burned
(d) meaning: a real stone broke the window

practice.question: Read the passage and give the meaning of each quoted word with the words that are its clue. “The market opened before dawn, and by sunrise it was teeming. Traders called from every corner, porters threaded through the crowd with loads balanced on their heads, and the air smelled of frying akara. Amina, who had arrived with an empty basket and a modest sum, moved from stall to stall, comparing prices and writing each one in a small book.” (a) teeming (b) modest (c) threaded
practice.answer: (a) Teeming — full of people and activity; clue: the traders calling from every corner and the crowd that the porters move through. (b) Modest — small, not large; clue: she arrived with an empty basket and spends her time comparing and recording prices, which fits a small amount of money. (c) Threaded — moved carefully through gaps in the crowd; clue: through the crowd with loads balanced on their heads.

marking.criterion: (a) meaning: full of people and activity
(a) clue: the traders calling and the crowd
(b) clue: the empty basket and careful price comparison
(c) meaning: moved carefully through the crowd
(c) clue: loads balanced on their heads as they pass through

practice.question: Write a full answer in the taught form for notorious: “The road became notorious for accidents, and drivers avoided it at night.” Include the word, its part of speech, its meaning in this sentence and the clue.
practice.answer: Notorious (adjective) — widely known for something bad; here the road was well known because of its accidents. Clue: “drivers avoided it at night” shows that its reputation was bad.

marking.criterion: word given with the part of speech: adjective
meaning: widely known for something bad
clue quoted from the sentence and linked to the bad reputation
meaning given as a short phrase, not a copied dictionary entry
